title: What Could Ancient Humans Do That We CAN'T?
title_alternatives: Ancient Skills Your Body Has FORGOTTEN
Did We Really Lose Our SUPERPOWERS?
The Children Who See Underwater: SEA Nomads
Which Human Abilities Are Truly GONE?
description:
Meet a child who can see clearly underwater. This video asks what ancient and traditional lifestyles could do that most of us can't: sea nomads' vision and spleens, Twa tree climbers, the Hadza gut, the Tsimane heart, Kalahari trackers, scent trails and cold sleeping.

This video is history and science, not medical advice.

Sources:
- Gislen et al. (2003). Superior underwater vision in a human population of sea gypsies. Current Biology.
- Gislen et al. (2006). Visual training improves underwater vision in children. Vision Research.
- Ilardo et al. (2018). Physiological and genetic adaptations to diving in sea nomads. Cell.
- Venkataraman, Kraft & Dominy (2013). Tree climbing and human evolution. PNAS.
- Smits et al. (2017). Seasonal cycling in the gut microbiome of the Hadza. Science.
- Kaplan et al. (2017). Coronary atherosclerosis in indigenous South American Tsimane. The Lancet.

scenes.narration: Meet a child who can see clearly underwater.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character swims underwater with eyes wide open, bubbles rising, a seashell on the sand below.

scenes.narration: Moken sea nomad children beat European kids underwater.
scenes.image_prompt: A spiral seashell on pale sand under clear blue water, light rays from above, no people.
scenes.fact_source: Gislen, Dacke, Kroger, Abrahamsson, Nilsson & Warrant (2003). Superior underwater vision in a human population of sea gypsies. Current Biology 13, 833-836

scenes.narration: So which ancient skills can't you do anymore?
scenes.image_prompt: The main character scratches his head in front of a blank stone wall, thinking hard.

scenes.narration: Some sea nomads have spleens about fifty percent bigger.
scenes.image_prompt: A simple bean-shaped organ glowing red on a plain pale background.
scenes.fact_source: Ilardo et al. (2018). Physiological and genetic adaptations to diving in sea nomads. Cell 173, 569-580

scenes.narration: Because your body may still hold skills you've never used.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character looks at his own open hands, curious, a soft glow around them.

scenes.narration: Twa climbers flex their ankles past forty-five degrees.
scenes.image_prompt: A bare ankle and foot pressed flat against a tall tree trunk, close up, rough bark.
scenes.fact_source: Venkataraman, Kraft & Dominy (2013). Tree climbing and human evolution. PNAS 110, 1237-1242

scenes.narration: By the end, you'll know which skills you can regain.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds up a single finger with a confident grin.

scenes.narration: Eighty-five percent of Tsimane adults had zero coronary calcium.
scenes.image_prompt: A simple heart drawn in clean red on a plain background, glowing softly.
scenes.fact_source: Kaplan et al. (2017). Coronary atherosclerosis in indigenous South American Tsimane: a cross-sectional cohort study. The Lancet 389, 1730-1739

scenes.narration: Is it evolution, or is it simply practice?
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stands at a fork in a dirt path, one way marked by a bone, the other by a footprint.

scenes.narration: Kalahari trackers helped build a computer with no words.
scenes.image_prompt: A small handheld computer showing only simple animal pictures as icons, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: CyberTracker Conservation (Louis Liebenberg with the University of Cape Town); Mail & Guardian and News24 reports (2003)

scenes.narration: So which skills are gone forever, and which aren't?
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds a key in one hand and looks at a locked wooden door.

scenes.narration: And European children learned the same underwater trick.
scenes.image_prompt: A bright swimming pool with light rays under the surface and a few bubbles rising, no people.
scenes.fact_source: Gislen, Warrant, Dacke & Kroger (2006). Visual training improves underwater vision in children. Vision Research 46, 3443-3450

scenes.narration: Let's start at the water, with the Moken, sea nomads who spend much of their lives on boats and islands in the Andaman Sea.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stands in a small wooden boat near green islands, shading his eyes with one hand.

scenes.narration: In two thousand three, Anna Gislen and colleagues tested seventeen Moken children and eighteen European children, all aged seven to thirteen, on what they could see underwater.
scenes.image_prompt: Two plain white cards with tiny black lines drawn on them lying on a pale seabed under clear water.
scenes.fact_source: Gislen, Dacke, Kroger, Abrahamsson, Nilsson & Warrant (2003). Superior underwater vision in a human population of sea gypsies. Current Biology 13, 833-836

scenes.narration: Seventeen kids against eighteen. I can barely read a menu without my glasses, never mind a seashell.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character squints hard at a tiny shell held at arm's length, tongue sticking out.

scenes.narration: Our eyes are built for air, so underwater things blur. The Moken children squeezed their pupils smaller, about one point nine six millimetres against two and a half, and focused as hard as a human eye can. The European children didn't.
scenes.image_prompt: A simple cutaway of an eye with a small round pupil and bent rays of light, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Gislen, Dacke, Kroger, Abrahamsson, Nilsson & Warrant (2003). Superior underwater vision in a human population of sea gypsies. Current Biology 13, 833-836

scenes.narration: So is it a special gene? That's what I assumed too. Here's the twist.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character raises one eyebrow and holds up a small DNA spiral, doubtful.

scenes.narration: In two thousand six, Gislen's team gave European children eleven underwater training sessions over about a month. Months later, tested again, they matched the Moken children's underwater sharpness.
scenes.image_prompt: A row of eleven small round stones on a rock above a clear blue pool, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Gislen, Warrant, Dacke & Kroger (2006). Visual training improves underwater vision in children. Vision Research 46, 3443-3450

scenes.narration: A skill we'd call lost wasn't gone. It was just never asked for, like a language you stopped speaking.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character swims confidently underwater holding a pearl-white shell, smiling, bubbles trailing.

scenes.narration: Now the Bajau, sea nomads of Indonesia. Melissa Ilardo scanned their spleens with ultrasound and found them about fifty percent larger than those of neighboring farmers.
scenes.image_prompt: A simple bean-shaped organ drawn large next to a smaller one on a plain pale background.
scenes.fact_source: Ilardo et al. (2018). Physiological and genetic adaptations to diving in sea nomads. Cell 173, 569-580

scenes.narration: Fifty percent. Honestly, I couldn't tell you where mine is.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character pokes his belly with a puzzled face, searching for something.

scenes.narration: Even Bajau who don't dive had big spleens, which points to genes. One gene, PDE10A, was linked to spleen size.
scenes.image_prompt: A short ladder of colored DNA blocks with one glowing block, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Ilardo et al. (2018). Physiological and genetic adaptations to diving in sea nomads. Cell 173, 569-580

scenes.narration: So this one isn't just practice. It's partly written in the family tree. I tried holding my breath in the bath once, gave up at twenty seconds and declared victory.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character studies a simple family tree drawn in chalk on a cave wall, nodding.

scenes.narration: Reports say Bajau divers have been seen going down about seventy metres. But their breath-hold times haven't been formally measured, and the thirteen minutes you may have heard is one diver's memory.
scenes.image_prompt: A rope line dropping from a small wooden boat into deep blue water with a glowing ring far below.
scenes.fact_source: Ilardo et al. (2018). Physiological and genetic adaptations to diving in sea nomads. Cell 173, 569-580

scenes.narration: Now let's go up. A real tree, with honey at the top and a very long way down.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stands at the foot of a huge tree, craning his neck up, a beehive far above.

scenes.narration: Vivek Venkataraman and colleagues studied the Twa hunter-gatherers of Uganda, who climb tall trees for honey, and compared them with their neighbors, the Bakiga farmers.
scenes.image_prompt: A very tall tree with a thick trunk and a small wild beehive in a high branch, under a bright sky.
scenes.fact_source: Venkataraman, Kraft & Dominy (2013). Tree climbing and human evolution. PNAS 110, 1237-1242

scenes.narration: I get nervous on a stepladder changing a light bulb.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character wobbles on a small stepladder holding a round bulb, knees shaking.

scenes.narration: The Twa bent their ankles past forty-five degrees while climbing, similar to wild chimpanzees. And their calf muscles had longer fibers than the farmers'.
scenes.image_prompt: A simple lower leg bone meeting a foot bone at a sharp angle, beside a tall tree trunk, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Venkataraman, Kraft & Dominy (2013). Tree climbing and human evolution. PNAS 110, 1237-1242

scenes.narration: Longer fibers mean a calf that stretches further. The authors argue that lets a climber keep their body closer to the trunk.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character hugs a tree trunk with both arms and legs, hanging close to the bark, concentrating.

scenes.narration: In the Philippines, the tree-climbing Agta also had longer calf fibers than their non-climbing neighbors, the Manobo.
scenes.image_prompt: Two simple rope bundles side by side, one clearly longer than the other, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Venkataraman, Kraft & Dominy (2013). Tree climbing and human evolution. PNAS 110, 1237-1242

scenes.narration: And here's the puzzle. The bones showed no matching signal. A skill like that can live entirely in soft tissue, and soft tissue vanishes from the fossil record.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds up a clean white leg bone and looks at it, then looks at his own calf, puzzled.

scenes.narration: One press report suggests the fibers may grow with practice. The researchers called that a suspicion, not a result.
scenes.image_prompt: A tall tree with a ladder of small branches going up, plain sky, no people.
scenes.fact_source: Venkataraman, Kraft & Dominy (2013). Tree climbing and human evolution. PNAS 110, 1237-1242

scenes.narration: Quick pause. If you're enjoying this, subscribe and stay with me. We'll keep digging into the ancient world together, one odd question at a time. It's free, it takes a second, and it helps other curious people find us.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character waves at the viewer with a warm smile, a small campfire glowing behind him.

scenes.narration: Next, something you can't see at all. Smits and colleagues collected three hundred and fifty stool samples from the Hadza over more than a year. Their gut bacteria cycled with the seasons, with some types vanishing and later coming back.
scenes.image_prompt: A simple calendar wheel drawn on a rock with four seasons colored green, gold, brown and blue, no letters.
scenes.fact_source: Smits et al. (2017). Seasonal cycling in the gut microbiome of the Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania. Science 357, 802-806

scenes.narration: A seasonal menu for your gut. Mine has two settings: pizza and leftover pizza.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character sits on a log holding a slice of pizza in each hand, grinning.

scenes.narration: The bacteria that cycled most in the Hadza were the same ones that separated industrial from traditional populations, across eighteen populations in sixteen countries.
scenes.image_prompt: Two sets of tiny colorful microbes, one rich and varied and one smaller, side by side on a plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Smits et al. (2017). Seasonal cycling in the gut microbiome of the Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania. Science 357, 802-806

scenes.narration: Now, honesty time. This one's contested, and I'd rather tell you that now than bury it later.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds a small cracked clay jar and tilts it, thoughtful.

scenes.narration: A preprint comment reanalyzed the same data and found weaker differences, with the seasonal signal driven by one window, when more meat was available.
scenes.image_prompt: A simple chart with two bars of different heights and a small red circle around the shorter one, no letters.
scenes.fact_source: Comment on 'Seasonal cycling in the gut microbiome of the Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania' (2018). bioRxiv preprint, not peer reviewed

scenes.narration: So I'd call it promising, not settled. Science that argues with itself is the kind I trust.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character gives a thoughtful thumbs-up beside a scroll with a small dent, smiling.

scenes.narration: Now the heart. Hillard Kaplan and colleagues scanned seven hundred and five Tsimane adults, aged forty and over, in the Bolivian Amazon. Eighty-five percent had no coronary calcium at all.
scenes.image_prompt: A red heart shape with a clean white outline, glowing softly, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Kaplan et al. (2017). Coronary atherosclerosis in indigenous South American Tsimane: a cross-sectional cohort study. The Lancet 389, 1730-1739

scenes.narration: Zero. For most of them. That's not a typo, and the number honestly made me read it twice.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stares at a big empty zero drawn in the dirt with a stick, stunned.

scenes.narration: The authors called it the lowest level of coronary artery disease reported in any population, and compared it with more than sixty-eight hundred people in a big American study. They suspect diet and a very active life.
scenes.image_prompt: A small clay bowl of tubers and beans beside a path winding through green jungle, no people.
scenes.fact_source: Kaplan et al. (2017). Coronary atherosclerosis in indigenous South American Tsimane: a cross-sectional cohort study. The Lancet 389, 1730-1739

scenes.narration: I'm not a doctor, and this isn't advice. It's just a reminder that a body built for a different life can behave very differently.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character raises both palms in a calm gesture, shaking his head gently, in warm light.

scenes.narration: But the same people face heavy infections. Research on the Tsimane found infections behind about half of the deaths documented.
scenes.image_prompt: A tiny green germ in a magnifying circle on a plain pale background.
scenes.fact_source: Gurven, M. et al., Tsimane Health and Life History Project: Social Science & Medicine 75 (2012) 2493-2502 (infections 55 percent of infant deaths); ScienceDaily (2009) report (half of documented deaths from infectious or parasitic disease)

scenes.narration: So ancient doesn't mean better. It means different, with its own price tags.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character holds a balance scale with a heart on one side and a tiny germ on the other.

scenes.narration: Now our eyes. In a two thousand eight study of six and seven-year-olds of Chinese ethnicity, nearsightedness was three point three percent in Sydney and twenty-nine point one percent in Singapore.
scenes.image_prompt: Two simple pairs of eyeglasses side by side, one pair on a small stack, the other pair on a much bigger stack, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Rose et al. (2008). Myopia, lifestyle, and schooling in students of Chinese ethnicity in Singapore and Sydney. Archives of Ophthalmology 126, 527-530

scenes.narration: Almost nine times as much. Same ethnicity. So it can't be just genes.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character looks from a tiny stack of glasses to a huge stack, stunned.

scenes.narration: The Sydney children spent about fourteen hours a week outdoors, the Singapore children about three. That was the strongest factor, though the authors also pointed to early schooling pressure.
scenes.image_prompt: A wide green field with a bright sun, a small bench and no people, plain horizon.
scenes.fact_source: Rose et al. (2008). Myopia, lifestyle, and schooling in students of Chinese ethnicity in Singapore and Sydney. Archives of Ophthalmology 126, 527-530

scenes.narration: I'd love to say I spend my days outside. I spend them staring at a glowing rectangle, and my eyes file a complaint every evening.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character stares cross-eyed at a flat glowing slab held very close to his face.

scenes.narration: And here's a skill that jumped straight into modern science. Louis Liebenberg worked with San trackers in the Kalahari and helped build CyberTracker, a handheld computer with picture icons, so trackers who don't read could record what they see.
scenes.image_prompt: A small handheld computer with a screen of simple animal icons, resting on warm desert sand.
scenes.fact_source: CyberTracker Conservation (Louis Liebenberg with the University of Cape Town); Mail & Guardian and News24 reports (2003)

scenes.narration: No words on the screen. Just animals, and what they're doing: drinking, feeding, running, fighting.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character taps a small flat screen with one finger, delighted, a trail of footprints behind him.

scenes.narration: Liebenberg has argued that the art of tracking may well be the origin of science. And by two thousand three, one report said conservationists in more than thirty countries were using the tool.
scenes.image_prompt: A wide world map drawn simply with many small dots glowing, plain background, no letters.
scenes.fact_source: Liebenberg, L. (1990). The Art of Tracking: The Origin of Science. David Philip; Liebenberg et al., papers on tracking as science (the art of tracking 'may well be the origin of science')

scenes.narration: Trackers read the ground like a living newspaper, and now rangers read the same news. Meanwhile, I can't find my keys in my own house.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character searches under a cushion and inside a boot with a puzzled face, a pile of stuff around him.

scenes.narration: What about smell? Porter and colleagues laid a ten-metre scent trail in a grass field and asked thirty-two blindfolded volunteers to follow it with their noses alone. About two thirds, twenty-one of them, made it to the end.
scenes.image_prompt: A thin curving trail of dark chocolate drops across a green field with a bright sky, no people.
scenes.fact_source: Porter et al. (2007). Mechanisms of scent-tracking in humans. Nature Neuroscience 10, 27-29

scenes.narration: Crawling on a lawn, sniffing chocolate. Honestly, I'd have signed up for free chocolate alone.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character crawls on the grass with a blindfold on, nose down, following a trail.

scenes.narration: Nobody succeeded with their nostrils taped, and two open nostrils were faster than one. Four volunteers who trained roughly doubled their speed within a few days.
scenes.image_prompt: A simple nose drawn large with two nostrils glowing on a plain background, a small arrow pointing at each, no letters.
scenes.fact_source: Porter et al. (2007). Mechanisms of scent-tracking in humans. Nature Neuroscience 10, 27-29

scenes.narration: So smell isn't gone. It's out of practice, like a muscle we stopped asking to work, and honestly it makes me want to go sniff something.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character sniffs a flower with a huge smile, eyes closed, in a sunny meadow.

scenes.narration: Then there's cold. In nineteen fifty-eight, Per Scholander and colleagues tested Aboriginal Australians sleeping on a cold desert night. They reported that the Aboriginal group slept soundly while European volunteers shivered and burned more energy.
scenes.image_prompt: A dry desert at night with a crescent moon, two small embers glowing in the sand, no people.
scenes.fact_source: Scholander, Hammel, Hart, LeMessurier & Steen (1958). Cold adaptation in Australian aborigines. Journal of Applied Physiology 13, 211-218

scenes.narration: A small, old study, and the set-up details differ between accounts, so I'd hold it loosely. But it hints our bodies can tune themselves to a harsh life.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character shivers under a thin blanket by a tiny fire, then yawns and smiles, tucked in.

scenes.narration: Back to the sea nomads. Outside researchers have said the spleen finding needs larger samples, and the thyroid explanation comes from mouse studies, not people.
scenes.image_prompt: A single small grey mouse standing beside a tiny scientific balance on a plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Ilardo et al. (2018). Physiological and genetic adaptations to diving in sea nomads. Cell 173, 569-580

scenes.narration: I like that. Scientists saying 'we don't know yet' out loud is a sign they're being straight with us.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character shrugs with a wide honest smile, palms open, beside a cave wall.

scenes.narration: The Moken study also showed the gain isn't general eyesight. The authors said it wasn't better contrast sensitivity overall. It's a specific trick, learned for a specific job.
scenes.image_prompt: A single pale seashell glowing in clear water with a thin circle of light around it, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Gislen, Warrant, Dacke & Kroger (2006). Visual training improves underwater vision in children. Vision Research 46, 3443-3450

scenes.narration: So here's my sorting of 'lost' abilities. Some are trainable, like underwater vision. Some are inherited, like that spleen. Some are lifestyle, like arteries and eyes. And a few left no trace in bone. Personally, the trainable ones are the part I find most hopeful.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character counts on his fingers, four of them raised, standing in front of a plain stone wall.

scenes.narration: Even so, the Tsimane also had high inflammation markers, about half of them, so their lives aren't a recipe for perfect health.
scenes.image_prompt: A simple thermometer with a red level on a stone, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Kaplan et al. (2017). Coronary atherosclerosis in indigenous South American Tsimane: a cross-sectional cohort study. The Lancet 389, 1730-1739

scenes.narration: Which is why I don't want to romanticize the past. A bad harvest or a bad infection could end a life.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character looks at an empty basket under a gray cloud, worried.

scenes.narration: Across twenty-one small-scale societies, adults who made it through childhood most often died at about seventy-two.
scenes.image_prompt: A tall bundle of many small candles glowing in a dark cave.
scenes.fact_source: Gurven & Kaplan (2007). Longevity among hunter-gatherers: a cross-cultural examination. Population and Development Review 33, 321-365

scenes.narration: The danger was early. Survive childhood, and an ancient life could stretch out nearly as long as ours.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character gently lights one small candle from another, a warm glow on his face.

scenes.narration: The Sydney Myopia Study, of thousands of children, found the lowest nearsightedness in twelve-year-olds with lots of outdoor time, however much close work they did.
scenes.image_prompt: A wide empty playground field with a bright sun and a lone swing, plain background, no people.
scenes.fact_source: Rose et al. (2008). Outdoor activity reduces the prevalence of myopia in children. Ophthalmology 115, 1279-1285

scenes.narration: So the cheapest ancient skill to get back might just be going outside. I'm writing this indoors. I know.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character steps through a doorway into bright sunshine, squinting and grinning, arms wide.

scenes.narration: And the Twa study's authors concluded that the ankle changes tied to walking upright remain compatible with vertical climbing, so we may have kept more of our old toolkit than we thought.
scenes.image_prompt: A simple ankle bone drawn in clean lines next to a small tree branch, plain background.
scenes.fact_source: Venkataraman, Kraft & Dominy (2013). Tree climbing and human evolution. PNAS 110, 1237-1242

scenes.narration: So what did we lose? Mostly not abilities, but practice. Some of it is genes, some is lifestyle, and some we'll never know, because it left nothing in bone. Thanks for spending these minutes with me. Hit like if you learned something, and tell me in the comments which of these you'd try first. I read every one. Next time, another strange question from the ancient world. See you soon, friend.
scenes.image_prompt: The main character waves goodbye at sunrise beside a small campfire, a bright sky behind him, smiling warmly.
